title: Nadar: the kindly glance
hook: effort matters, but the Granth speaks of grace, the Beloved's glance, as what finally opens the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam; your line was the name fills you. That closes a week: ang, every page a limb; bani, a weaver's songs beside a king's; mahala, every guru signs as nanak; hukam, living in tune; haumai, the cure is inside; and naam. Today, a glance.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME FILLS YOU.` → `A WEEK: ANG, BANI, MAHALA, HUKAM, HAUMAI, NAAM.`

segments.voice: A school play. A nervous kid in the back row has rehearsed for weeks, knows every line, and still freezes when the lights come up. Then they catch a parent's eye in the audience, and the parent gives the smallest nod. That's all. And the kid breathes, and speaks. All the practice mattered. But it was the glance that opened the door.
screen: `A NERVOUS KID ON STAGE.` → `ONE GLANCE, ONE NOD.` → `THE DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is nadar. It comes from the Persian nazar: sight, a look, a glance. In the Granth it means the Beloved's kindly glance: grace, given, not earned. Once you know the word, you'll find it everywhere. The Mool Mantar ends with gur prasaad: by the Guru's grace. Pauri 4 of the Japji puts it in one line: karmee aavai kaparraa, nadaree mokh duaar. By your deeds comes this garment, this life, this body. By the glance of grace comes the door of liberation. Pauri 32, where you climbed the ladder of the Name, ended: Nanak nadaree paaeeai, by grace it's reached. And the last pauri, the goldsmith's shop, closed with nadaree nadar nihaal: with a glance, the Gracious One fills them with joy. So the Granth holds two things together, and it's worth being careful here. Effort matters. The Gurus worked, served, sang, and taught others to live honestly and remember the Name. The ladder is real, and you climb it. But climbing isn't the same as arriving. The door opens by nadar. The glance isn't a reward you can demand, like a paycheck. It's more like the nod from the audience, from someone who has been watching with love all along. In the Granth's picture, you do your part, and the door is not yours to force.
screen: `NADAR — A GLANCE, FROM NAZAR.` · `NADAREE MOKH DUAAR.` · `EFFORT CLIMBS; GRACE OPENS.` · `NOT A PAYCHECK, A NOD.` · then, large: `THE GLANCE COMES.`

segments.voice: Think of one good thing in your life you didn't earn: a person who loves you, your health today, a chance someone gave you before you deserved it. Let yourself feel thankful, not for your own effort but for the gift. If you pray, thank the One for it silently, in your own way; if not, let the thanks sit warm in your chest, and breathe with it.
Nadar. The kindly glance: grace, given, not earned. Effort climbs the ladder, and in the Granth, the glance is what opens the door.
Your line: the glance comes. You do your part; the door opens by grace. A full week, closed with a glance.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace, as the last words of the Mool Mantar, and many speak of any good outcome as coming through the Guru's kirpa, grace, while still working hard for it.

chat.says: If grace can't be earned, why do Sikhs work so hard at their practice?
options: Effort matters, but the door opens by nadar: a glance that's given, not earned.
They're earning it: with enough effort, grace has to be handed over.
Because nadar means effort; the harder you climb, the more you've got.
